questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The commonest leukaemia in children is:
questions.concept: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia accounts for about 80% of childhood leukaemia, peaking at 2 to 5 years, and B-cell precursor ALL with hyperdiploidy carries the best prognosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukaemia represents:
questions.concept: The Philadelphia chromosome is a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 creating the BCR-ABL1 fusion tyrosine kinase, the target of imatinib. It is present in over 95% of CML.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Auer rods in the bone marrow are characteristic of:
questions.concept: Auer rods are crystallised azurophilic granules seen in myeloblasts, most abundant in acute promyelocytic leukaemia. They confirm a myeloid rather than lymphoid lineage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia is treated with which differentiating agent?
questions.concept: All-trans retinoic acid overcomes the PML-RARA mediated block in myeloid differentiation and, with arsenic trioxide, has made APL the most curable AML. It also reverses the associated disseminated intravascular coagulation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Reed-Sternberg cells are the hallmark of:
questions.concept: Reed-Sternberg cells are large binucleate owl-eye cells expressing CD15 and CD30, diagnostic of Hodgkin lymphoma. Nodular sclerosis is the commonest subtype and lymphocyte predominant has the best prognosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The starry-sky appearance on histology with t(8;14) and a very high proliferation rate indicates:
questions.concept: Burkitt lymphoma shows sheets of monomorphic cells with interspersed pale macrophages producing the starry-sky pattern, driven by MYC translocation to the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus, and is associated with EBV in the endemic African jaw form.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The diagnostic triad of multiple myeloma includes monoclonal gammopathy, lytic bone lesions and:
options: Clonal plasma cells in the marrow of 10% or more
questions.concept: Diagnosis requires 10% or more clonal marrow plasma cells or a plasmacytoma plus a myeloma-defining event: hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia or lytic bone lesions (the CRAB criteria). Alkaline phosphatase is typically normal as there is no osteoblastic activity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Smudge cells and absolute lymphocytosis with CD5-positive, CD23-positive B cells in an elderly man indicate:
questions.concept: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is the commonest leukaemia of the elderly, showing mature small lymphocytes with smudge cells and co-expression of CD5 with CD19, CD20 and CD23. It may be complicated by autoimmune haemolysis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which finding on serum protein electrophoresis suggests multiple myeloma rather than a reactive process?
options: Diffuse polyclonal increase in gamma globulins
A dense narrow M-band with suppression of other immunoglobulins
questions.concept: A monoclonal M-band with immunoparesis of the uninvolved immunoglobulin classes indicates a clonal plasma cell disorder, unlike the broad polyclonal rise of chronic infection or inflammation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Rouleaux formation on a peripheral smear with a very high erythrocyte sedimentation rate is typical of:
questions.concept: High circulating paraprotein neutralises the negative surface charge of red cells, causing rouleaux and a markedly raised ESR - a classical clue to myeloma alongside bone pain and renal failure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Haemophilia A results from deficiency of:
questions.concept: Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive deficiency of factor VIII causing deep muscle and joint bleeding with a prolonged APTT and normal prothrombin time and platelet count. Haemophilia B is factor IX deficiency.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The commonest inherited bleeding disorder is:
questions.concept: von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, usually autosomal dominant, causing mucocutaneous bleeding with a prolonged bleeding time and often a mildly prolonged APTT because vWF carries factor VIII.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: In disseminated intravascular coagulation, which combination is expected?
options: Prolonged PT and APTT, low platelets, low fibrinogen, raised D-dimer
Normal PT, low platelets, raised fibrinogen
Prolonged PT only with normal platelets
Isolated prolonged APTT with normal D-dimer
questions.concept: DIC consumes platelets and clotting factors while activating fibrinolysis, so PT and APTT are prolonged, platelets and fibrinogen fall and D-dimer rises. Treatment is of the underlying cause with replacement of components as needed.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura characteristically shows:
options: Isolated thrombocytopenia with increased megakaryocytes in marrow
questions.concept: ITP is antibody-mediated peripheral platelet destruction, so the count is low but marrow megakaryocytes are normal or increased, and the rest of the counts are normal. Schistocytes would suggest a microangiopathy instead.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A prolonged prothrombin time that corrects on mixing with normal plasma indicates:
questions.concept: Correction on a mixing study indicates deficiency of a clotting factor, since normal plasma supplies the missing factor. Failure to correct suggests an inhibitor such as a lupus anticoagulant or an acquired factor VIII antibody.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The most common inherited thrombophilia in the Indian population is:
questions.concept: Factor V Leiden, which renders factor Va resistant to inactivation by activated protein C, is the commonest inherited thrombophilia, though it is less prevalent in South Asians than in Europeans. Antithrombin deficiency is rarer but more thrombogenic.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Heparin therapy is monitored by:
questions.concept: Unfractionated heparin potentiates antithrombin III and is monitored by the APTT, targeting 1.5 to 2.5 times control. Low molecular weight heparin needs no routine monitoring, and warfarin is monitored by INR.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The antidote for warfarin over-anticoagulation with major bleeding is:
options: Intravenous vitamin K with four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
questions.concept: Major warfarin-related bleeding is reversed with intravenous vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate for immediate factor replacement. Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is characterised by:
options: Bleeding due to platelet destruction within 24 hours
Thrombocytopenia with paradoxical thrombosis 5 to 10 days after starting heparin
questions.concept: Antibodies to the heparin-platelet factor 4 complex activate platelets, causing a falling count with arterial and venous thrombosis rather than bleeding, typically 5 to 10 days after exposure. Heparin must be stopped and a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban started.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Aspirin produces its antiplatelet effect by:
questions.concept: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, abolishing thromboxane A2 synthesis for the platelet lifespan of 7 to 10 days, which is why it is withheld before surgery. Clopidogrel blocks P2Y12 and abciximab blocks GpIIb/IIIa.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The cardinal features of Parkinson's disease are:
options: Resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and postural instability
questions.concept: Parkinson's disease results from loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, producing an asymmetrical pill-rolling rest tremor at 4 to 6 Hz, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia and later postural instability.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Parkinson Disease and Other Movement Disorders

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The most effective drug for symptomatic relief in Parkinson's disease is:
questions.concept: Levodopa combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor remains the most effective treatment; carbidopa prevents peripheral conversion, reducing nausea and allowing more levodopa to reach the brain. Long-term use brings dyskinesias and on-off fluctuations.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Huntington disease is characterised by:
options: Autosomal recessive inheritance with copper deposition
Autosomal dominant CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion with caudate atrophy
questions.concept: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant, caused by CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4, with anticipation, and shows chorea, dementia and psychiatric disturbance with atrophy of the caudate producing box-car ventricles.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Parkinson Disease and Other Movement Disorders

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A young patient with tremor, dysarthria, Kayser-Fleischer rings and deranged liver function most likely has:
questions.concept: Wilson disease is autosomal recessive ATP7B deficiency causing copper accumulation, with Kayser-Fleischer rings, low serum ceruloplasmin, raised urinary copper and lentiform nucleus degeneration. Penicillamine or trientine with zinc is used.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Parkinson Disease and Other Movement Disorders

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which is the commonest cause of dementia?
questions.concept: Alzheimer disease accounts for 60 to 70% of dementia, with amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau, hippocampal atrophy and an insidious amnestic onset. Vascular dementia is second and typically stepwise.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Parkinson Disease and Other Movement Disorders

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Early prominent visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition and marked neuroleptic sensitivity suggest:
questions.concept: Dementia with Lewy bodies features fluctuating cognition, vivid visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and REM sleep behaviour disorder, with severe sensitivity to antipsychotics that can precipitate rigidity. Alpha-synuclein inclusions are the pathological hallmark.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Parkinson Disease and Other Movement Disorders

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: The classical triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus is:
options: Gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and dementia
questions.concept: Normal pressure hydrocephalus presents with a magnetic gait, urinary incontinence and cognitive slowing with ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy. It is potentially reversible by ventriculoperitoneal shunting, and gait improves first.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Parkinson Disease and Other Movement Disorders

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Vertical gaze palsy with early falls, axial rigidity and poor levodopa response indicates:
questions.concept: Progressive supranuclear palsy (Steele-Richardson-Olszewski syndrome) causes supranuclear vertical gaze palsy, early postural instability with backward falls, axial rigidity and a poor levodopa response, with tau pathology and midbrain atrophy.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Parkinson Disease and Other Movement Disorders

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Hemiballismus results from a lesion of the:
questions.concept: Violent flinging movements of one half of the body follow a lesion, usually a lacunar infarct, of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, which normally provides excitatory drive to the globus pallidus internus.
questions.reference: HARR 21e, Parkinson Disease and Other Movement Disorders

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Which drug commonly causes drug-induced parkinsonism?
questions.concept: Typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol block striatal D2 receptors and produce a symmetrical parkinsonism, as do metoclopramide and prochlorperazine. It is reversible on withdrawal and treated with anticholinergics rather than levodopa.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Demyelinating disease, spinal cord syndromes & headache
questions.stem: Multiple sclerosis is best diagnosed by demonstrating lesions disseminated in:
questions.concept: Diagnosis rests on dissemination in space and time, shown clinically or by MRI lesions in characteristic periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal locations, with oligoclonal bands in cerebrospinal fluid supporting it.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Demyelinating disease, spinal cord syndromes & headache
questions.stem: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia in a young woman suggests a lesion of the:
questions.concept: Failure of adduction of one eye with nystagmus of the abducting eye indicates a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion, and when bilateral in a young adult is highly suggestive of multiple sclerosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Demyelinating disease, spinal cord syndromes & headache
questions.stem: The treatment of choice for an acute relapse of multiple sclerosis is:
questions.concept: High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone shortens the duration of an acute relapse though it does not alter long-term disability. Interferon beta and other agents are disease-modifying rather than relapse treatments.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Demyelinating disease, spinal cord syndromes & headache
questions.stem: Brown-Sequard syndrome from hemisection of the spinal cord produces:
options: Ipsilateral loss of proprioception and motor power with contralateral loss of pain and temperature
Loss of pain and temperature with preserved motor power
questions.concept: Hemisection interrupts the ipsilateral corticospinal tract and dorsal columns, which have already decussated or do so higher, and the spinothalamic tract that has crossed from the opposite side - giving the classical dissociated picture one or two segments below.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Demyelinating disease, spinal cord syndromes & headache
questions.stem: A syringomyelia typically causes:
options: Cape-like loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch
questions.concept: A central cavity first interrupts the decussating spinothalamic fibres in the anterior white commissure, producing a suspended cape-like loss of pain and temperature with sparing of the dorsal columns - dissociated sensory loss.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Demyelinating disease, spinal cord syndromes & headache
questions.stem: Anterior spinal artery occlusion spares:
questions.concept: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord, so infarction causes paraplegia with loss of pain and temperature and sphincter disturbance while the posteriorly supplied dorsal columns, and therefore proprioception and vibration, are spared.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Demyelinating disease, spinal cord syndromes & headache
questions.stem: A strictly unilateral, severe, throbbing headache with photophobia, nausea and preceding visual aura is:
questions.concept: Migraine with aura gives a unilateral pulsatile headache lasting 4 to 72 hours with photophobia, phonophobia and nausea, preceded by a spreading visual aura. Triptans treat the attack and propranolol or topiramate prevent it.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Demyelinating disease, spinal cord syndromes & headache
questions.stem: Severe strictly unilateral periorbital pain lasting 30 to 90 minutes with lacrimation, conjunctival injection and ptosis, recurring nightly in clusters, is treated acutely with:
questions.concept: Cluster headache responds acutely to 100% oxygen and subcutaneous sumatriptan, with verapamil for prophylaxis. Indomethacin is the specific treatment for paroxysmal hemicrania and carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Demyelinating disease, spinal cord syndromes & headache
questions.stem: Neuromyelitis optica is distinguished from multiple sclerosis by antibodies against:
questions.concept: Anti-aquaporin-4 IgG targets astrocytic water channels, producing longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis with severe optic neuritis. Distinguishing it matters because interferon beta worsens neuromyelitis optica.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Demyelinating disease, spinal cord syndromes & headache
questions.stem: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord affects predominantly the:
questions.concept: Vitamin B12 deficiency demyelinates the posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, giving loss of vibration and joint position sense with a positive Romberg sign, spastic weakness and extensor plantars despite absent ankle reflexes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Coma, raised intracranial pressure & brain death
questions.stem: The lowest possible score on the Glasgow Coma Scale is:
questions.concept: The scale scores eye opening 1 to 4, verbal response 1 to 5 and motor response 1 to 6, so the minimum total is 3 and the maximum 15. A score of 8 or below defines coma and usually mandates airway protection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Coma, raised intracranial pressure & brain death
questions.stem: Cushing's reflex in raised intracranial pressure consists of:
questions.concept: The Cushing response is systemic hypertension with bradycardia and irregular breathing, a late and ominous sign of critically raised intracranial pressure that heralds herniation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Coma, raised intracranial pressure & brain death
questions.stem: Uncal (transtentorial) herniation classically first compresses which cranial nerve?
questions.concept: The uncus compresses the third nerve against the petroclinoid ligament, so the earliest sign is an ipsilateral dilated poorly reactive pupil, followed by ptosis and a down-and-out eye, then contralateral hemiparesis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Coma, raised intracranial pressure & brain death
questions.stem: Which measure most rapidly lowers acutely raised intracranial pressure?
options: Intravenous mannitol with head elevation and controlled hyperventilation
questions.concept: Osmotic diuresis with mannitol or hypertonic saline, 30-degree head elevation and short-term controlled hyperventilation act within minutes. Dexamethasone helps only vasogenic oedema around tumours and has no role in trauma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Coma, raised intracranial pressure & brain death
questions.stem: Decorticate posturing (flexion of the upper limbs with extension of the lower limbs) localises the lesion:
options: Above the midbrain, in the cerebral hemispheres or internal capsule
questions.concept: Decorticate rigidity indicates a lesion above the midbrain with release of the rubrospinal tract, and carries a better prognosis than decerebrate extensor posturing, which implies brainstem involvement at or below the midbrain.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Coma, raised intracranial pressure & brain death
questions.stem: Pinpoint pupils with respiratory depression and coma suggest:
questions.concept: The triad of coma, pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression is classical of opioid overdose, reversed by naloxone. Organophosphates also cause miosis but with fasciculations and profuse secretions.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Coma, raised intracranial pressure & brain death
questions.stem: Doll's eye movement (oculocephalic reflex) is absent when there is:
questions.concept: The oculocephalic reflex requires intact vestibular nuclei, medial longitudinal fasciculus and third and sixth nerve nuclei, so its loss in a comatose patient indicates brainstem failure. It is testable only after excluding cervical spine injury.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Coma, raised intracranial pressure & brain death
questions.stem: Which is required before a diagnosis of brain death can be made?
options: A confirmatory electroencephalogram in all cases
Absence of sedatives, normothermia, normal electrolytes and a known irreversible cause
questions.concept: Prerequisites are a known irreversible catastrophic brain injury with exclusion of confounders - drugs, hypothermia, severe metabolic or endocrine disturbance and hypotension - before testing brainstem reflexes and apnoea. Spinal reflexes may persist and do not exclude brain death.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Coma, raised intracranial pressure & brain death
questions.stem: The apnoea test in brain death certification is considered positive when:
options: No respiratory effort occurs despite arterial PCO2 rising above 60 mmHg
questions.concept: Absence of any respiratory effort despite an arterial PCO2 above 60 mmHg, or a rise of 20 mmHg above baseline, confirms loss of the medullary respiratory centre. The test is abandoned if the patient becomes unstable.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Coma, raised intracranial pressure & brain death
questions.stem: A patient is awake with preserved eye opening and vertical gaze but is unable to move or speak. This is:
questions.concept: Locked-in syndrome follows a ventral pontine lesion, usually basilar artery occlusion, sparing the reticular formation and the vertical gaze centres, so consciousness is intact and communication is possible through vertical eye movements and blinking.
